sections.title: Mishnah: Two Holding a Garment, Each Claiming It
sections.gist: Two litigants hold one item, and neither has proof. Each swears to the smallest share he claims, and they divide it. The Mishnah covers equal claims, a whole-versus-half claim, an animal ridden or led, and when no oath is needed.

bullets.text: *Bava Metzia*, the 'middle gate', is the second of Nezikin's three parts. *Bava Kamma* is built around damages, but *Bava Metzia* ranges widely: contested ownership and found objects, interest, bailees and workers' rights.
Tosafot: the tractate opens here because *Bava Kamma* ended with dividing items between two parties, the shavings left between a craftsman and his employer.

The Mishnah makes two moves. First, it divides the item at all, because both litigants are *muchzak* (in possession, and so presumed owner). Second, it words the oath so that it matches the ruling exactly.

children.title: Why Two Who Each Claim the Whole Garment Swear to 'No Less Than Half'
children.gist: Each litigant says he found the garment and it is all his. Each swears he owns no less than half, and they divide it. The shiur explains why the oath is worded this way, and what an oath achieves when one side may be lying.

bullets.text: Mishnah: two come to court holding a garment. Each says 'I found it' and 'All of it is mine.' Each swears *she'ein lo bah pachot me'chetzyah* (that he owns no less than half of it), and they divide it.
Dividing is the natural result: the claims are equal, both are holding it, and there is no evidence. In practice one buys out the other's half, or they sell it and split the money.

Why not have each swear 'it is all mine'? Then the court would be making at least one of them swear falsely. Swearing 'half is mine' would make each give up his own claim. 'No less than half' is true for an honest claimant, and it matches the ruling exactly, since each takes half.

What does the oath achieve? The working assumption, *chashud a'mamona lav chashud a'shevuata* (one suspected about money is not suspected about oaths): a man who would grab a garment may still refuse to swear falsely, and so he backs down.

More often the oath is aimed at *mori ve'amar* (rationalizing: talking oneself into a permissive ruling). The grabber is usually no brazen thief. He has persuaded himself he saw it first or deserves it more, and the gravity of a formal oath breaks through that story.

children.title: One Claims All, the Other Half, and Only the Disputed Half Is Divided
children.gist: The one who claims half concedes the other half, so only one half is in dispute, and it is split. The oaths match the result: the first swears to no less than three-quarters and takes them, the second to no less than a quarter and takes it.

bullets.text: Mishnah: one says 'All of it is mine' and the other 'Half of it is mine.' Since both agree that half belongs to the first, they argue only over the other half.
The first swears he owns no less than three-quarters, the second that he owns no less than a quarter. The first takes three-quarters and the second a quarter.

Tosafot asks: the half-claimant could have said 'all of it is mine' and received half. Why doesn't that *migo* (since he could have made a stronger claim, his weaker claim is believed) give him the full half he claims?

Tosafot's answer: the claimant of the whole is *muchzak* in all of it, while the half-claimant is *muchzak* only in half. His *migo* would take the disputed quarter out of the other's possession, and a *migo le'hotzi* (a *migo* used to extract from another's possession) doesn't work, since *ha'motzi me'chavero alav ha'ra'ayah* (whoever takes from another must bring proof).
So the division is driven by possession together with the claims. Where neither side holds the item, as with a boat the Gemara discusses later, the result may be no division at all.

children.title: Riding or Leading an Animal Counts Like Holding It
children.gist: Two people riding an animal, or one riding and one leading it by the halter, each claim all of it. The ruling is the same: each swears to no less than half, and they divide.

bullets.text: Mishnah: whether both are riding, or one rides and the other leads the animal, each swears that he owns no less than half of it, and they divide it.

The new point is what kind of contact counts as possession. Riding and leading are forms of control different from gripping a garment, and the Mishnah shows by example, without stating a rule, that both are enough.

children.title: No Oath When They Admit Each Other's Claims or Have Witnesses
children.gist: If the litigants admit each other's claims, or witnesses back them, they divide without an oath. An oath is imposed only when there is no other way to establish the facts.

bullets.text: Mishnah: when they admit to each other's claims, or each has witnesses, they divide without an oath. The oath was there only to bring out the truth, and here the truth is already known.

sections.title: Why Each Litigant Says Both 'I Found It' and 'All of It Is Mine'
sections.gist: The Gemara asks why each litigant makes two statements. A first answer reads them as one claim, with 'All of it is mine' added to teach that *re'iyah* does not acquire. Rav Pappa instead finds two cases, a find and a purchase, and the Gemara explains why each needs the oath.

children.title: Seeing a Lost Object Does Not Acquire It
children.gist: The first answer reads the two statements as one claim: 'I found it, and so all of it is mine.' 'All of it is mine' is added because 'I found it' could mean 'I saw it', and *re'iyah* alone does not acquire.

bullets.text: Why two statements for each litigant? Let the Mishnah state one. Answer: it is one claim: 'I found it, and all of it is mine.'

Then let him say only 'I found it', and we would know he means it is all his. But 'I found it' could mean 'I saw it': he saw it first and thinks *re'iyah* (seeing an object) acquires it. The Mishnah adds 'All of it is mine' to teach that seeing alone does not acquire.
Objection: can 'found' mean 'saw'? Rabbenai reads 'which he has lost, and you have found it' (Devarim 22:3) to mean that it came into his hands.
Answer: in the verse it does mean possession. But the Mishnah speaks in everyday language, where a person who has only seen an item says 'I found it'.
Think of a parking space: in ordinary speech, spotting it first feels like a claim before you have pulled in. The Mishnah heads off that reading.

Then let him say only 'All of it is mine'. The Gemara answers that the Mishnah needs both: 'I found it' sets the case among found items, and 'All of it is mine' shows that he means he took it, since seeing alone does not acquire.

children.title: Rav Pappa: A Find and a Purchase Are Two Separate Cases
children.gist: The Gemara rejects the single-claim reading, since the Mishnah repeats 'this one says' for each statement. Rav Pappa explains that the first clause is about a found item and the second about an item each says he bought.

bullets.text: The Mishnah introduces each statement with its own 'this one says… and that one says', so these are two separate claims, not one compound claim.

Rav Pappa (some say Rav Shimi bar Ashi, some say it is unattributed): the first clause, 'I found it', concerns a found item. The second, 'All of it is mine', concerns buying and selling, where each says he is the one who bought it from the seller.

children.title: Why Both a Find and a Purchase Call for an Oath
children.gist: In each case a claimant can talk himself into seizing the item, but for a different reason. With a find, he tells himself the other finder had nothing before. With a purchase, he tells himself the other buyer can just buy another. Taught alone, either case would suggest the other needs no oath.

bullets.text: Had the Mishnah taught only the find, we would say the oath belongs there alone. The claimant can tell himself: 'The other loses nothing, since it was never his. I'll seize it and share it.' In a purchase that excuse isn't available, so we might think there is no oath.

Had it taught only the purchase, we would say the oath belongs there. He can tell himself: 'He paid and I paid. Now that I need it, I'll take it, and he can go to the trouble of buying another.' In a find that can't be said, so we might think the Sages didn't suspect him and imposed no oath.

This is *mori ve'amar*. The oath is aimed less at the knowing liar than at the man who has half-convinced himself that his claim is fair. Each case makes a different excuse available, so each must be taught.

Where no excuse is available, the claimant is either a brazen thief or sincerely mistaken. Neither is likely to back down because of an oath, which is why one might have thought no oath is needed there.

children.title: The Seller Who Took Money from Both Buyers
children.gist: Why not settle the purchase case by asking the seller whose money he took? Because he took money from both, from one willingly and from the other against his will, and no one knows which was which, so only an oath can clarify it.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks: in a purchase, let us see whose money the seller took; that buyer bought it. Answer: he took money from both. He accepted it willingly from the one he wanted to sell to and against his will from the other, and it is not known which is which, so the matter goes to an oath.

Tosafot considers whether the confused seller could serve at least as a single witness, which would change who must swear. In the case as framed he truly can't recall, so the dispute returns to two equal, unsupported claims.

sections.title: Can the Mishnah's Oath Fit Ben Nannas and Sumakhos?
sections.gist: The Gemara tests the Mishnah's oath against two *tanna'im* who limit oaths. Ben Nannas won't impose an oath that one side must be swearing falsely, and Sumakhos divides doubtful property with no oath at all. The Ben Nannas question is answered at once; the Sumakhos question draws two answers and a *kal va'chomer* that carries onto 3a.

children.title: Ben Nannas: No Oath Where One Side Must Be Lying
children.gist: Ben Nannas objects to having both the storekeeper and the laborer swear, since one of them is certainly lying. The Mishnah can still follow him: the two may have lifted the garment together, so both oaths may be true.

bullets.text: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah doesn't follow Ben Nannas, who won't administer an oath to two parties when one of them is certainly lying.

Mishnah (the Rabbis, Shevuot 45a): an employer tells his laborer, 'Go to the storekeeper and he will give you food for your wages.' The storekeeper says he gave it, and the laborer says he received nothing. Both swear, and the employer pays them both.

Ben Nannas: how can both come to a *shevuat shav* (an oath in vain, here one certainly false)? One of them must be lying. By the same logic, the finders, who divide the garment anyway, should take their shares without an oath.

The Gemara rejects the suggestion: there, one oath is certainly false. Here both may be true, because they may have lifted the garment together and each owns half, so Ben Nannas would agree that they swear.
Lifting together is not the likeliest story, but it is a real possibility. Ben Nannas objects only to an oath that must be false, not to one that may be false.

children.title: Sumakhos: Doubtful Property Is Divided Without an Oath
children.gist: Sumakhos rules that *mamon ha'mutal be'safek* is divided with no oath, so the Mishnah's oath seems not to fit him. The Gemara first limits his rule to two *shema* claims, then, for Rabba bar Rav Huna, to cases of *derara de'mamona*, and meets that answer with a *kal va'chomer*.

bullets.text: Sumakhos holds that *mamon ha'mutal be'safek* (property of doubtful ownership) is divided without an oath. His classic case: a cow is sold and a calf is found beside it, and no one knows whether it was born before the sale or after. The Rabbis leave it with the seller unless the buyer brings proof; Sumakhos divides it.

children.title: Both Holding the Garment Fits the Rabbis but Seems to Exclude Sumakhos
children.gist: The Gemara argues that the Mishnah fits the Rabbis, not Sumakhos. The Rabbis demand proof only when one side holds the property; when both hold it, they divide with an oath. Sumakhos divides without an oath even when they don't both hold it, so all the more so should he divide the garment without one.

bullets.text: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah doesn't follow Sumakhos, who divides doubtful property without an oath.
Counter: then whom does it follow, the Rabbis? They hold *ha'motzi me'chavero alav ha'ra'ayah*, and here neither side brings proof, yet the garment is divided.

The Gemara answers: the Rabbis can distinguish. There, the two aren't both holding the property, so the one in possession keeps it and the claimant must prove his case. Here both are holding it and neither has it alone, so they divide, with an oath.
In other words, for the Rabbis possession decides who is the claimant. Where only one side is *muchzak*, the other bears the burden of proof; where both are, the division is the default.

But Sumakhos faces a *kal va'chomer* (a fortiori argument): if he divides without an oath where they aren't both holding it, then here, where both are holding it, all the more so should they divide without an oath.

children.title: Sumakhos Divides Without an Oath Only Between Two Shema Claims
children.gist: First answer: Sumakhos divides without an oath only when neither side claims to know, *shema* against *shema*. When both make certain claims, *bari* against *bari*, as the finders do, he too requires an oath.

bullets.text: The Mishnah can follow Sumakhos. His rule applies to *shema* (perhaps: an uncertain claim) against *shema*, when neither party can say for certain that the property is his. With *bari* (a certain claim) against *bari*, he doesn't divide without an oath.

The logic: in the calf case no one saw the birth, so there is nothing either side could truthfully swear to. A definite claim can carry a definite oath, and that oath may still bring a rationalizer to admit.

children.title: Sumakhos Divides Without an Oath Only Where There Is Derara de'Mamona
children.gist: Rabba bar Rav Huna holds that Sumakhos divides without an oath even between two *bari* claims. The Gemara answers that he does so only where there is *derara de'mamona*, a stake in the item apart from the claims; the finders have none, so they swear.

bullets.text: The Gemara asks: Rabba bar Rav Huna says that Sumakhos divides without an oath even with *bari* against *bari*. How does the Mishnah fit Sumakhos by his account?

Answer: Sumakhos divides without an oath only where the litigants have *derara de'mamona* (a monetary stake in the item apart from their claims). Where they have nothing but their claims, they don't divide without an oath.

Tosafot: *derara de'mamona* means that the agreed facts alone raise a question of ownership. In the calf case everyone agrees the cow was sold and the calf was born, and only the timing is unknown, so an outsider would see the doubt.

In the garment case the agreed facts show only two people holding a garment. The doubt exists only because of what they claim, and that is just where an oath, which works against rationalizing, is needed.

children.title: Why Swear When the Garment May Truly Belong to Both?
children.gist: The Gemara objects with a *kal va'chomer*. Where each has a stake, the item surely belongs wholly to one of them, and Sumakhos still divides it without an oath; here it may truly belong to both, so all the more should they divide without one.

bullets.text: The Gemara: where each litigant has *derara de'mamona*, the item may belong wholly to one or wholly to the other, and Sumakhos still divides it without an oath. Here, with no stake, it may well belong to both. Is it not all the more so that they should divide it without an oath?

The force of the argument: splitting the calf is certainly not *ke'fi ha'emet* (true to the facts), since a calf can't belong to both, yet Sumakhos rules so without trying an oath. Splitting the garment may be exactly the truth, so it should need an oath even less.

returns_to.note: A second kal va'chomer against Sumakhos, now aimed at the derara de'mamona answer

children.continues: Continues on 3a: the Gemara answers that this oath is a rabbinic enactment, instituted so that people won't go and seize another's garment and say 'It is mine.'

key_terms.definition: The party in possession of disputed property, who is presumed to own it until the other side proves otherwise.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Both finders are holding the garment and so are equally in possession, which is why the Mishnah divides it; the Rabbis demand proof only where one side alone holds the property.

key_terms.sense: burden of proof on the claimant
key_terms.definition: The basic rule of civil procedure: whoever seeks to take property from another's possession must bring proof.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Rabbis apply it to doubtful property that only one side holds; when both hold the item, they divide it with an oath.

key_terms.definition: Merely seeing an ownerless or lost object, as distinct from taking hold of it. Seeing alone does not acquire.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara's first answer explains 'All of it is mine' as teaching that a finder who only saw the item first has not acquired it.

key_terms.definition: A person talking himself into a permissive ruling for his own benefit, convincing himself that taking something is justified, as distinct from knowingly stealing.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara shows that a find and a purchase each offer the claimant his own excuse, so the Sages impose an oath in both.

key_terms.definition: An oath taken in vain, including one that is certainly false.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Ben Nannas won't have both the storekeeper and the laborer swear, since one oath must be false; the finders' oaths may both be true.

key_terms.definition: Property whose ownership between two parties is in genuine doubt. Sumakhos divides it between them; the Rabbis leave it with its holder unless the other brings proof.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Sumakhos divides such property without an oath, which seems to clash with the Mishnah's oath.

key_terms.definition: A *bari* claim is one the litigant asserts as known fact ('it is certainly mine'); a *shema* claim is one he can only put as a possibility ('perhaps it is mine').
key_terms.on_this_daf: By the Gemara's first answer, Sumakhos divides without an oath only between two *shema* claims, not two *bari* claims like the finders'.

key_terms.sense: a monetary stake apart from the claims
key_terms.definition: A doubt about ownership that arises from the agreed facts themselves, giving each side a stake in the property independent of what he claims.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara limits Sumakhos's division without an oath to cases with *derara de'mamona*, which the finders lack, and then challenges that answer with a kal va'chomer.

sages.name: Sumakhos
sages.full_name: Sumakhos (the tanna, student of R. Meir)

quiz.q: Two people come to court holding a garment, and each says, 'I found it, and all of it is mine.' What does the Mishnah rule?
options: Each swears he owns no less than half, and they divide it
Each swears it is all his, and they divide it
They divide it without an oath
It is set aside until one of them brings proof
quiz.why: Swearing to 'no less than half' neither forces an honest claimant to lie nor makes him give up his claim, and it matches the ruling: each takes half.

quiz.q: One litigant holding a garment claims all of it, and the other claims half. How is it divided?
options: Three-quarters to the one who claims all, a quarter to the other
Half to each
All of it to the one who claims all
It is left with whoever grips it more firmly
quiz.why: The half-claimant concedes half, so only the other half is in dispute, and that half is split between them.

quiz.q: By the Gemara's first answer, why does each litigant add 'All of it is mine' to 'I found it'?
options: To teach that *re'iyah*, merely seeing a lost object, does not acquire it
To teach that a find needs witnesses
Because in the Torah 'finding' means seeing
To show that each claims a different half
quiz.why: In everyday speech 'I found it' can mean 'I saw it'; 'All of it is mine' shows he means he took hold of it, since seeing alone does not acquire.

quiz.q: Two people each say they bought the same item from a seller. How, according to the Gemara, might one of them talk himself into seizing it?
options: 'We both paid the seller; I need it, so let him go to the trouble of buying another'
'The other loses nothing, since it was never his'
'The seller will say I paid first'
'An oath about a purchase is never taken'
quiz.why: Since the loser can buy another, the claimant can tell himself he isn't really taking anything. That excuse is what makes the oath needed in a purchase.

quiz.q: Why can't the court settle the purchase case by asking the seller whose money he took?
options: He took money from both, one willingly and one against his will, and no one knows which
A seller is never believed about his own sale
The seller has an interest in the outcome
The buyers paid through an agent
quiz.why: With money in hand from both and no way to know whose he accepted willingly, the seller can't decide it, so the dispute goes to an oath.

quiz.q: Ben Nannas objects when both the storekeeper and the laborer swear, since one must be lying. Why can the Mishnah's oath still fit his view?
options: The finders may have lifted the garment together, so both oaths may be true
The Mishnah's oath is only rabbinic
The finders have witnesses
Ben Nannas objects only to oaths over food
quiz.why: Ben Nannas rejects an oath that is certainly false. If they lifted it together, each truly owns no less than half.

quiz.q: By the Gemara's first answer, when does Sumakhos divide doubtful property without an oath?
options: Only when both claims are *shema*, uncertain
Whenever ownership is in doubt, even with certain claims
Only when both are holding the item
Never: he always requires an oath
quiz.why: An uncertain claim can't support an oath, but between two *bari* claims, like the finders', Sumakhos too requires one.

quiz.q: Rabba bar Rav Huna holds that Sumakhos divides without an oath even between two certain claims. Why, then, do the finders still swear?
options: They have no *derara de'mamona*, no stake in the item apart from their claims
Because both are holding the garment
Because one of them is certainly lying
Because a find is easy to rationalize
quiz.why: Sumakhos divides without an oath only where the doubt comes from the facts themselves; here it comes only from what the finders claim.

judgment_calls: The Mishnah's four cases are children of one Mishnah section rather than four top-level sections, since they are variations on one rule (both hold, neither has proof, swear to the minimum, divide).
The first single-claim answer (2a.5–2a.9), including Rabbenai's verse, is one section rather than a parent with a Rabbenai child; a child in the middle would have pushed the 2a.9 step out of order.

The seller who took money from both (2b.3) is its own section, separate from the rationalization discussion it follows, because it answers a separate objection to the purchase reading; it could also have been a bullet in that section.
Ben Nannas and Sumakhos are grouped under one top-level section, since the Gemara tests both in the same way ('let us say the Mishnah doesn't follow…'); each could also stand alone.

2b.7–2b.10 (the Rabbis' distinction and the first kal va'chomer) is kept as one section because the Gemara builds it as a single argument; the alternative was separate sections for the Rabbis and the kal va'chomer.
The second kal va'chomer (2b.14–3a.1) is linked by returns_to to the first, as both press Sumakhos with the same kind of argument.
coverage_notes: The essay attributes the exegesis of 'and you have found it' to Ravina; the text has Rabbenai. Followed the text.

The essay presents the shema/bari limit and the derara de'mamona limit as two successive points; the text brings derara de'mamona only to answer Rabba bar Rav Huna, who holds that Sumakhos divides even between bari claims. Followed the text; Rabba bar Rav Huna is not mentioned in the essay.

The essay describes a single kal va'chomer after the derara de'mamona answer; the text has two, one at 2b.10 (both holding vs. neither holding) and one at 2b.14–3a.1 (a stake vs. no stake). Outlined both in the text's order.

The essay frames the 2b.14 kal va'chomer partly as Sumakhos 'taking from a chazakah'; the text frames it as an item belonging wholly to one vs. possibly to both. Followed the text, keeping the shiur's 'ke'fi ha'emet' framing as shiur.
The calf-and-cow case for Sumakhos is not in the text of these lines; it comes from the shiur and is marked as shiur.
The essay's Ben Nannas case mentions 'a hundred dinars'; the text gives no sum. Left it out.
The shiur's answer to the kal va'chomer (R. Yochanan's rabbinic enactment, 3a.2) lies outside this scope; mentioned only in 'continues', without the name.
The shiur's overview of Bava Metzia and Tosafot on the connection to the end of Bava Kamma are included as detail-3 shiur bullets.

Sage list: 'Rav' (2a.11) is a false match for Rav Pappa, and 'Rav Huna' (2b.12) a false match for Rabba bar Rav Huna; both were given id null with full names. Sumakhos and Rabbenai were missed by the list.
